The Wall Street Journal earlier this year sought to tackle a vexing question: how can we capture the conversations ricocheting around the country? Not just in one state, but everywhere?

   So far, we’ve found: 

   1. MAGA influencers who played a huge role in propelling President Trump in 2024 are largely tuning him out in 2026. Instead, many conservative podcasters have devoted more time to criticizing James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate. They also spent a tremendous amount of time discussing a Massachusetts murder trial.

Why is this notable? We are trying to understand what the country cares about and what is motivating voters before they cast their ballots. Will a fixation on Talarico drive voters to the polls in just Texas? Or will that inspire GOP voters in other states too? And if they aren’t discussing Trump as much as they did a couple of years ago, does that mean GOP enthusiasm and turnout might be lower than when he was on the ballot in 2024?

   2. Many Americans seem to hate AI. It’s sort of incredible to use AI to discover how much Americans are talking about their hatred of AI, but welcome to 2026. In this fascinating visual story , we found that backlash to AI and Flock Safety cameras had united an unusual coalition of TikTok creators from both the left and the right. And this angst is animating people who usually steer clear of politics.

AI, data centers and a number of other debates about technology have jumped into the political discourse in ways few expected. Many politicians from both parties have been caught flat footed by the backlash. Perhaps this all manifests itself in the 2026 elections, but the snowballing populism could show itself in an even bigger way in 2028.

Many politicians from both parties have been caught flat footed by the backlash. Perhaps this all manifests itself in the 2026 elections, but the snowballing populism could show itself in an even bigger way in 2028.

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Kimberly Guilfoyle: Top Democrats on the House and Senate foreign affairs committees have urged the State Department to review the actions of the U.S.’s ambassador to Greece over her efforts to promote gas deals with a Greek company.

 

Jobs: The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release September’s job numbers at 8:30 a.m. ET.

What I’m Following

 
 
BETTMANN ARCHIVE/GETTY IMAGES
 

The Justice Department is considering whether prosecutors mistreated Richard Nixon. The reputation of the former president, who quit the White House over the Watergate affair, is enjoying a renaissance among some Republicans. Now the Justice Department is considering whether the special counsel’s office that investigated the infamous Watergate break-in committed misconduct, more than half a century later.

 

The U.S. is sending a third aircraft-carrier group to the Middle East. The Pentagon is sending the aircraft-carrier strike group and additional Marine Corps ships to the region, adding 9,000 to 10,000 more troops to the more than 50,0000 already in place. Trump is weighing renewed strikes on Iran after next month’s midterm elections.

Dan Sullivan touted the investment in an LNG pipeline project during an Oval Office appearance on Wednesday. It appears to have one hitch, however: South Korea didn’t agree to a specific dollar figure—or even to invest at all.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Local police are raking in as much as $2 million for each arrest in Trump’s immigration crackdown.

 

• Senate Democrats are challenging the legality of the Pentagon’s plan to take a stake in a Venezuelan oil company, laying the groundwork for a potential probe.

 

• The Treasury Department will let married couples count as two taxpayers for a novel school-choice tax credit, significantly expanding a program.

 

• A judge in Washington has barred the Trump administration from any future attempt to charge a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
